title: How Tibo Louis-Lucas built and sold Tweet Hunter and Taplio: ship fast, charge early, stay lean
summary: Tibo explains why two VC-backed startups failed (no focus on revenue, big teams that couldn't pivot) and how he then shipped about 10 small projects in 4 months to find Tweet Hunter. He covers charging early, giving creators a small product stake for distribution, SEO mini-tools, and structuring the exit.

principles.text: Judge a business by revenue, not vanity metrics like signups; users who don't pay are false reassurance.
principles.quote: you are not revenue-driven, you are not 100% focused on revenue (translated from French)

principles.text: Raising money and hiring a big team blocks fast pivots; staying solo or tiny lets you test ideas quickly.
principles.quote: raising money and hiring a big team completely stops you from pivoting quickly and working on the latest idea you had (translated from French)

principles.text: Compress a two-year failure into a week by shipping many tiny products fast and killing what doesn't earn.
principles.quote: the goal was to try to compress those 2 years into one week (translated from French)

principles.text: Ask for payment very early on every product, since willingness to pay is the real validation.
principles.quote: very, very early in the process, on every product, we asked people to pay (translated from French)

principles.text: Create distribution when small by giving big creators a tiny stake in the product with no formal obligations.
principles.quote: we told them: we give you 0.1% of Tweet Hunter, and in exchange you have no concrete obligation (translated from French)

principles.text: Build free SEO mini-tools from your product's features; their traffic compounds over time and feeds the main product.
principles.quote: the traffic from these mini tools will compound and become more and more important (translated from French)
